summary: The Pallavas ruled from Kanchipuram from the late 3rd century, first issuing grants in Prakrit and surviving a raid by the Gupta emperor Samudragupta and the Kalabhra upheaval. Revived by Simhavishnu in the later 6th century, they fought the Chalukyas of Vatapi for more than a century, sacking Vatapi in 642 and building the temples of Mamallapuram and Kanchi. Pressed by the Chalukyas, Rashtrakutas and Pandyas, they finally lost their kingdom when the Chola Aditya I killed the last king, Aparajita, in 897.
details: The origins of the Pallavas are debated: they may have begun as feudatories of the Satavahanas, as a local family of the Kanchi region, or as a people of pastoral descent. Their earliest records are three copper-plate grants in Prakrit issued from Kanchipuram by King Sivaskandavarman. One, the Hirahadagalli plates, is dated to 283 CE, in his eighth regnal year. These grants show a dynasty already established at Kanchipuram, a city that would remain the Pallava capital for more than six centuries.

In the 4th century the Gupta emperor Samudragupta (c. 335–375) led a campaign into the Deccan and the south. His Allahabad Pillar inscription lists Vishnugopa of Kanchi, probably a Pallava regent ruling for his nephew, among twelve southern kings he captured and then released as an act of favour. Most scholars think these kings were restored as tributaries, but some argue that Samudragupta never got beyond the Krishna river and that the boast covers a retreat. Either way, the Pallavas kept their kingdom, and the southern kings were never under direct Gupta rule.

In the 5th and 6th centuries the Pallavas lost ground: the Vishnukundins took lands in the north, and in the 6th century the Kalabhra invasions threw the Tamil country into upheaval. Late in the 6th century Simhavishnu, whose dates are disputed but are often given as c. 575–600, struck at the Kalabhras and restored Pallava power around Kanchi. The Pandya king Kadungon did the same in the south, and the Tamil country was divided between the Pallavas in the north and the Pandyas around Madurai. His revival began the age of the great Pallava kings.

Simhavishnu's son Mahendravarman I (c. 600–630) expanded the kingdom, but his reign also opened a long struggle with the Chalukyas of Vatapi in the Deccan, whose king Pulakeshin II invaded the Pallava north. Mahendravarman is remembered above all as a patron of the arts. He began the Pallava tradition of temples cut into solid rock, and he is credited with writing the Sanskrit comedy Mattavilasa Prahasana, which pokes fun at Buddhist and Shaiva ascetics. The rivalry with the Chalukyas would shape Pallava history for the next century and a half.

Narasimhavarman I came to the throne in 630. Pulakeshin II raided the Pallava north again but failed to take Kanchipuram, and Narasimhavarman beat the Chalukyas in several battles, including one at Manimangalam, about 20 miles east of Kanchi. He then carried the war into the Deccan. In 642 his army, led by the general Paranjothi, captured the Chalukya capital Vatapi (Badami), and Pulakeshin was killed. Narasimhavarman took the Tamil title Vatapikondan, 'he who conquered Vatapi', and the city never became a capital again.

Narasimhavarman I completed the monuments that his father had begun at the port of Mamallapuram, which was named in his honour, among them the group of temples known as the Pancha Rathas. In 640 the Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang had visited Kanchipuram, the Pallava capital. Narasimhavarman also twice sent an army to Sri Lanka to help the Sinhalese prince Manavarman, who had lived at his court, win the island's throne; the second expedition succeeded. Under him the Pallavas were at the peak of their power and fame.

After Mahendravarman II's brief reign, Paramesvaravarman I (c. 670–695) ruled, and in his time inscriptions in both Sanskrit and Tamil became common. His son Narasimhavarman II, known as Rajasimha (c. 695–728), is remembered as a builder in stone. He raised the Shore Temple at Mamallapuram, on the edge of the Bay of Bengal, and the Kailasanatha temple at Kanchipuram, one of the finest Pallava monuments, dates from his reign. His son Paramesvaravarman II ruled only briefly, and with his death in 731 the main line of the Pallavas came to an end.

When Paramesvaravarman II died without an heir, the throne passed to a collateral line. Nandivarman II, the son of Hiranyavarman of the Kadava family, was crowned at Kanchipuram while still a boy; one Chalukya account calls him a 13-year-old at the time of their invasion. His reign, which lasted until about 796, was one of the longest in Pallava history, but it was also full of danger, as the Chalukyas sought revenge for Vatapi and the Rashtrakutas rose in the Deccan. He took the title Pallavamalla.

The Chalukyas had never forgotten the sack of their capital. Their king Vikramaditya II (c. 733–744) invaded the Pallava kingdom with help from the Western Gangas; the earliest record of the campaign, the Narwan plates, dates to 741 or 742. The young Nandivarman II fled Kanchipuram after a brief defence, leaving his regalia and war elephants behind. Vikramaditya 'entered Kanchi without destroying it', spared its people, returned spoils to the temples and made gifts recorded in a Kannada inscription in the Kailasanatha temple. The Chalukyas took Kanchi three times in all.

Nandivarman III, son of Dantivarman, ruled from about 846 to 869. The Pandya king Srimara Srivallabha had pushed into Pallava country, and Nandivarman formed a coalition with the Rashtrakutas and the Western Gangas against him. At Tellaru the allies defeated the Pandyas and chased them south to the Vaigai river; one account dates the battle to 830, before his accession, so its year is uncertain. Srimara later recovered most of his lands. Nandivarman kept a strong navy, and a Tamil inscription at Takua Pa in Thailand points to Pallava-era trade with South-east Asia.

After Nandivarman III his sons divided the kingdom, and its last king, Aparajita, ruled from about 880. The Pallavas' Chola feudatories had grown strong, and their king Aditya I (c. 871–907), once a Pallava ally, turned against his overlords. In 897 he invaded Tondai Nadu, the Pallava heartland around Kanchipuram, and killed Aparajita in battle. Tondaimandalam became part of the Chola realm, and Aditya went on to conquer the Kongu country. The Pallava dynasty, which had ruled from Kanchi for six centuries, came to an end.
